newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Russian Gazprom's Trojan horse in Hungary.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian Gazprom's Trojan horse in Hungary.

text.p: A joint venture between Hungary's MOL and Russia's Gazprom might prove to be the opportunity for the Russian giant to challenge MOL's dominance of Hungary's lucrative domestic gas market.
The stakes are high because gas accounts for more than a third of Hungary's energy production.

In the first half of 1996 gas sales, which MOL now handles exclusively, totalled 6.9 billion cubic metres, of which 65 percent came from the Commonwealth of Independent States. Consumption is expected to grow from 10 billion cubic metres to 13 to 14 billion cubic metres a year within 15 years.
The joint venture, Panrusgaz, became a force to be reckoned with after it acquired the exclusive right to import gas from the former Soviet fields of Yamburg and Orenburg and sell it on to MOL.
The contracts were formerly held by Mineralimpex, a foreign trade company set up in the communist era to help MOL's international financial activities and bought out by MOL in 1994.
Lajos Antal, Panrusgaz's deputy general director, told Reuters the company plans eventually to sell directly to the customer without passing through MOL.

"We plan to sell gas to the big industrial consumers by the turn of the century," he said, adding that Gazprom has earmarked $450 million to build a gas pipeline from Slovakia to Italy with adjacent underground storage capacity by the first quarter of 1999.
MOL and Gazprom are expected to decide on the building of the Hungarian section later this year, he said.

Gazprombank, Gazprom's financial arm, also made its first step in Hungary by acquiring Altalanos Ertekforgalmi Bank, the new management of which has already said it intends to finance the gas pipeline project.
Frances Cloud of Nomura Securities Research believes such moves by Gazprom make it vital for MOL to keep its stake in Panrusgaz at the present 50 percent.
"I believe that MOL will do its best to keep its 50 percent stake in Panrusgaz, and if that means putting in more money or assets...I think it will do that," said the London-based analyst.
According to Antal, this will involve an injection of $25 million either in cash or assets.
MOL vice-president Tibor Gulyas also sees the day when the relationship with Gazprom becomes more competitive, especially if Panrusgaz is allowed to sell gas directly to the customer.

"MOL's gas supplier status at the moment is quite clear. If and when other companies meet the same requirements, the question of competition could arise," he said. "In the mid-term the relation will probably be a mix of partnership and competition."

Until now, the partnership has proved to be lucrative only for Gazprom, which in the first half of this year sold gas to MOL through Panrusgaz at a profit but which MOL resold at state-controlled prices for 2.4 forints ($0.153) per cubic metre less than it paid for it.

MOL suffered a 14.5 billion forint ($92.12 million) loss in the gas business in 1995 and said earlier this year it expects a 2.5 billion forints ($15.88 million) loss for 1996. Even that estimate could prove conservative following the government's decision last month to postpone until January 1 energy prices rises expected for October 1.
Analysts believe another consequence of the new Russian foothold in the Hungarian gas market could be a less successful second phase of MOL's privatisation, due later this year.
"With the arrival of competition, it is difficult to feel optimistic about the company's prospects in the forthcoming struggle for market share," said a recent Nomura Equity Research report.
The state privatisation agency APV RT still holds 58.6 percent of MOL, which has a registered capital of 98.4 billion forints ($625.1 million).
